text:
The report lists three discrepancies, all introduced when the slide was last packed: a sandbag left inside, a hose not torqued correctly on the aspirator, and incorrect material behind the aspirator. These point to a faulty overhaul or packing rather than a part failing in service, so the best fit is MISOVERHAULED. FOD (the sandbag) and UNDERTORQUED (the hose) each cover only one of the three issues.

MISOVERHAULED

The circuit breaker D6 was found pulled and collared, which caused the failure to pressurize. The label that matches this condition is PULLED.

PULLED

Holes found "out of standard" under the static discharger base point to a defect that was discovered rather than wear or corrosion. Of the available labels, DAMAGED fits best, though OUT OF LIMITS was a close alternative.

DAMAGED

Similar nose-gear-disagree reports involving strut servicing or replacement were labeled FAILED, so this one fits the same pattern.

FAILED

Uncommanded shutdown of engine #2 with no indications; the label that fits best is AUTO SHUTDOWN.

AUTO SHUTDOWN

Key details in the report:
- The left ram air deflector door was found not locked into position.
- The system was then placed on the MEL, locked in the flight open position.
- A test flight verified the left pack was not the source of the vibrations.

The defect actually found was the door not being locked, which points to UNLOCKED. The vibration troubleshooting itself was inconclusive. One could argue for NON ISSUE, since the door was not the cause. However, the discrepancy reported on the part was still "not locked."

UNLOCKED

The trim ran out of nose-down authority, and the fix was to rerig the pitch trim. That points to the trim being out of rig, so OUT OF RIG fits best.

OUT OF RIG

The defect that explains the symptoms is the #2 brake, which was found seized and replaced. A seized part maps most closely to STUCK, though FROZEN is a possible alternative.

STUCK

Several cautions appeared as the helicopter passed a 5G tower, the autopilot upper modes dropped out, and everything returned to normal on its own afterward. That fits a transient malfunction better than a hard failure. The closest example report (multiple autoflight cautions that cleared) was labeled MALFUNCTIONED. INTERMITTENT and ERRATIC were also possible fits.

MALFUNCTIONED

Lights stayed illuminated with power off; similar cases where lights remained on and an inertia switch was reset were labeled INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

The wire was checked and found routed correctly, with no defect and the aircraft returned to service. That makes this a non-issue.

NON ISSUE

The report describes a disbond in the horizontal stabilizer upper and lower skins at the rear spar. "Disbond" corresponds to two labels on the list, DEBONDED and UNBONDED. DEBONDED is the closer match to how such a finding would normally be labeled.

DEBONDED

Excessive build-up on the latch pin points to dirt as the cause, so this matches the dirt-related examples.

DIRTY

Two wires at the indicator connector were found in each other's pin positions (pin 14 instead of 7, and pin 7 instead of 14), so the fault is incorrect pinning. MISPINNED fits better than MISWIRED.

MISPINNED

Fuel pressure light illuminated; no cause found. Likely "WARNING LIGHT" or "LOW PRESSURE". The light indicates low fuel pressure, and the report centers on the annunciator illuminating, so I'll go with WARNING LIGHT.

WARNING LIGHT

The IDG oil level was found below the green band and was serviced, so the condition is low quantity. "LOW QUANTITY" fits better than plain "LOW", although the similar reports used LOW and LOW PRESSURE. The finding here is specifically the oil level, so LOW QUANTITY.

LOW QUANTITY

The core defect is that the MRO did the repair without approved data, leaving the shaft without its two oil lubrication holes. The oil leak is a symptom of that faulty repair, so the root condition is a repair error.

MISREPAIRED

Re-rigging the door fixed it, which points to OUT OF RIG or OUT OF ADJUST. The similar cases, where adjustment cured a handle popping up, were labeled OUT OF ADJUST. Here the action was explicitly "performed rig on left aft entry door," so OUT OF RIG fits best.

OUT OF RIG

Most similar examples (N1 would not reach target thrust, HMU/fuel pump replaced) were labeled INOPERATIVE.

INOPERATIVE

Masks deployed due to depressurization, so the deployment was intended. Either DEPLOYED or DISCHARGED fits, since the generators were discharged. The part condition is that the masks deployed, and the closest example (an intended deployment with masks repacked) was labeled DEPLOYED.

DEPLOYED

The fueler left the refuel/defuel switch on, which made the tank indication erratic. The cause is a ground handler's mistake, not a part defect, so HANDLER ERROR fits best.

HANDLER ERROR

Two holes on the rib were misdrilled, which points to a manufacturing defect, so the closest label is MISMANUFACTURED.

MISMANUFACTURED

The report says the R1 slide pack gauge was in the red on the over-pressure side, so the reported condition is high pressure. The inspection found the cylinder within limits, but the label describes the reported condition.

HIGH PRESSURE

The autopilot was unstable on AP1: speed swung from Mach .75 to .80, altitude varied by about 80 feet, and thrust cycled from full power to near idle. Troubleshooting found no fault and all computers passed the AFS test. That points to erratic behavior rather than a confirmed hard failure, so ERRATIC fits better than FAILED or MALFUNCTIONED.

ERRATIC

The left engine fan cowls were lost during takeoff, meaning they separated from the aircraft in flight. That fits INFLT SEPARATION better than MISSING.

INFLT SEPARATION

Life raft stowage came open and could not be re-stowed. The closest label is "DID NOT STOW", though "OPEN" and "IMPROPER STOW" are also candidates. Since the key point is that it would not stow again, I'll go with "DID NOT STOW".

DID NOT STOW

The right engine fuel flow transmitter read 0.2 lower than the left, while the fuel stick check confirmed the actual quantities were correct. That points to the transmitter reading inaccurately low, so the specific label is READS LOW rather than a general fault label.

READS LOW

Like the similar brake grabbing and chattering reports, this one describes brakes that chattered and handled roughly, and troubleshooting found air in the system. That pattern is labeled ABNORMAL or FAULTED in the examples. "CHATTERING" also exists as a label, but the closest examples used ABNORMAL, so I chose that.

ABNORMAL

Insect stuck in pitot probe. Prior examples labeled debris as OBSTRUCTED, and metallic debris (clogged) also as OBSTRUCTED, while another case was labeled FOD. An insect inside the probe is foreign matter blocking it, so OBSTRUCTED fits best.

OBSTRUCTED

The nose gear strut was found bottomed out, with no chrome showing, and the fix was servicing the strut. A strut that needs servicing because it bottomed out points to the strut being underserviced.

UNDERSERVICED

Wrong-length fasteners installed points to a maintenance installation error. Of the candidate labels, IMPROPER PART fits better than MISINSTALLED or INCORRECT, because the defect is the fastener itself (wrong length) rather than how it was fitted.

IMPROPER PART

The light was flickering on, which points to an intermittent condition. The fix was swapping the temperature sensor and replacing the cannon plug, consistent with an intermittent connection.

INTERMITTENT

The defect is a repair filler that does not meet the size required by the engineering authorization. That points to the repair being done wrong, and of the candidate labels (OUT OF TOLERANCE, MISREPAIRED, INCORRECT), MISREPAIRED fits a nonconforming repair best.

MISREPAIRED

Sparks were visible, but the report attributes the window replacement to arcing: the left side window heat element rang out open, and the controller was replaced "as a precaution due to window arcing." The condition of the failed part is therefore arcing, and ARCED is a label on the list.

ARCED

Across every disconnect method tried, the autopilot would not disengage, so the condition is a failure to respond to commands rather than a stuck button or a simple failure. UNRESPONSIVE fits; MALFUNCTIONED and FAILED were the other candidates.

UNRESPONSIVE

Misdrilled points to a manufacturing defect, which maps to MISMANUFACTURED. It could also be a repair error, but nothing in the report indicates a prior repair.

MISMANUFACTURED

Engine 1 only reached 1.2 EPR at takeoff power, while engine 2 was normal at 1.46, so the engine did not produce rated thrust. Fault isolation found a fault code, and the high power assurance test was then normal. The closest condition is a loss of power.

POWER LOSS

Options: IMPROPER PART, WRONG PART, INCORRECT. The mask has an incorrect part number, and "WRONG PART" fits a mask that was installed with the wrong part number.

WRONG PART

Similar "ship XXXX -brk/fire-" reports are split between DAMAGED and FIRE. This one explicitly reports brake fires at the #3 and #4 brakes, so FIRE fits best.

FIRE

The existing seat track repair was found not in conformity with the SRM because the wrong fasteners had been used, and the correct fasteners were then installed. That points to INCORRECT or IMPROPER PART. Since the report specifically says "fasteners incorrect," INCORRECT matches the wording most directly.

INCORRECT

The report's failed item is circuit breaker B7 (bleed air valves right), which was found open and reset, after which the operational check was normal. A similar report with a popped breaker that was simply reset was labeled TRIPPED. The choice here is between "OPEN" and "TRIPPED". Since the breaker had tripped and only needed a reset, TRIPPED fits best.

TRIPPED

Only a loud bang and a brief yaw are reported, with no failure or damage identified. This is closest to the earlier "momentary partial power loss with yaw kick" report, which was labeled ABNORMAL.

ABNORMAL

The "too low gear" audio alert sounded even though the gear showed down with three greens. That makes it a spurious warning from a component that was then replaced. Candidate labels are FALSE INDICATION, WARNING MESSAGE, MALFUNCTIONED and FAULTY. FALSE INDICATION fits best because the alert contradicted the actual gear state.

FALSE INDICATION

Debris was found stuck in front of the forward static port, which obstructed it. Candidate labels are FOD, OBSTRUCTED, BLOCKED and CONTAMINATED. Debris stuck in the port best fits OBSTRUCTED.

OBSTRUCTED

The detector worked correctly: it triggered briefly from what was likely someone vaping in the lavatory, and the test passed with no faults. That rules out a false indication or a part defect. The smoke itself was the real event, and among the available labels SMOKE fits better than ODOR or VAPOR.

SMOKE

The door would not arm, and the fix was simply re-engaging the girt bar mechanism, which means the mechanism had come out of engagement. The closest label is DISENGAGED.

DISENGAGED

The failed part is the load compressor plug, which was found "with threads damaged inside load compressor." Thread damage on a plug points to a stripped or damaged condition. STRIPPED fits damaged threads most specifically, though DAMAGED is the more literal wording in the report. I chose the more specific label.

STRIPPED

The left engine reached only 88% N1 and did not make takeoff power, so the defect is a loss of power. The EEC was deferred under the MEL, but the closest-fitting label for the observed condition is "POWER LOSS".

POWER LOSS

The report says all four LRRA antenna screws were found below 30 inch-lbs and were torqued back to spec, so the defect is insufficient torque.

LOW TORQUE

The report describes compliance with the inspection order and replacement of the bearing fittings, but it never says what condition was found. The most similar reports, which also give no specific defect, were labeled DAMAGED.

DAMAGED

Number 1 engine oil pressure stayed abnormally high, at 119 to 120 psi, until power was reduced, and the engine was removed and replaced. Of the candidate labels, HIGH PRESSURE describes this condition most directly.

HIGH PRESSURE

The report describes an APU fire indication in flight, but no fire was found. The cause was a failed APU fire detector giving a false warning, so the label is false indication.

FALSE INDICATION

Panels departing the engine is a separation, but the report could also be read as DAMAGED. The failed parts are the panels themselves, which came off the engine, so the condition is that they separated. "Upon landing" points to INFLT SEPARATION rather than SEPARATED, because the panels departed while the aircraft was moving.

INFLT SEPARATION

Similar reports where arcing was followed by the window shattering were labeled DAMAGED. The ones labeled ARCED described arcing with no window damage. This report has arcing and the window later cracked, so it matches the DAMAGED pattern most closely.

DAMAGED

The report describes thumps in flight and excess play in the left nose gear door. The fix was adjusting the uplock switch and the actuator door, which was found too tight, and tightening a clevis bolt. That makes the condition a rigging/adjustment issue, and "OUT OF ADJUST" fits best.

OUT OF ADJUST

The girt bar was not seated on the milled section and had to be realigned and reinstalled correctly. That points to an installation fault, which matches the similar "installed incorrectly" report labeled MISINSTALLED.

MISINSTALLED

This is a fuel imbalance / migration report where the readings did not agree with the fuel flows, and the left defuel valve and right fueling shutoff valve were replaced. The closest precedent is the most similar example, which describes an imbalance case and is labeled OUT OF BALANCE. Other similar migration cases were labeled INOPERATIVE, so that label was also possible.

OUT OF BALANCE

Dust was cleaned out of the flap handle, and a similar example with cleaning was labeled DIRTY. The PCB replacement could also be read as UNSERVICEABLE, but the dust in the handle is the specific defect noted, so DIRTY fits best.

DIRTY

The flight attendant could not disarm the door because a flap was getting in the way. The fix was to check and secure that flap, so the part's condition is interference rather than looseness.

INTERFERENCE

Bird struck inside the #2 engine inlet, with a loud bang, yaw and a burning smell in the cabin, which points to engine ingestion. Similar reports with bird remains in the engine were labeled BIRD INGESTION. Others labeled DAMAGED even when no damage was found.

BIRD INGESTION

Replacing the bracket and target, then performing a slat rig and sensor adjustment, points to the sensor or bracket being out of rig or out of adjustment. The closest similar report, where the proximity sensor dimension was corrected, was labeled OUT OF ADJUST. "OUT OF RIG" is also plausible here since a slat rig was done, but the sensor adjustment favors OUT OF ADJUST.

OUT OF ADJUST

Fuselage skin puncture repaired with a doubler. "PUNCTURED" is a valid label, but in the similar examples a puncture was labeled "DAMAGED", so this report follows the same convention.

DAMAGED

Debris was found in the captain's pitot tube and purged, which points to a blocked or clogged tube. Similar reports with debris or blockage were labeled CLOGGED or OBSTRUCTED, and CLOGGED fits debris best.

CLOGGED

Every similar SB388 report with scuffed and scored push rods and rocker arms is labeled DAMAGED. This report describes the same scoring on the same parts. The submitter suspects insufficient lubrication, which might suggest LACK OF LUBE or SCORED, but the observed condition matches the precedent.

DAMAGED

Maintenance ran an operational check, found the door working normally and recorded "no fault found," so no defect was confirmed. That points to NON ISSUE rather than a failure condition.

NON ISSUE

An existing doubler that does not comply with the approved ETD guidelines matches the pattern of non-conforming existing repairs. Those examples are labeled MISREPAIRED, although one similar case was labeled DAMAGED.

MISREPAIRED
